Interactive online appendix: an embedding map and type gallery of school imagery used to measure school characteristics in the Manta school-choice study.

School imagery — online appendix

Gregory Elacqua, Isabel Jacas, Thomas Krussig, Carolina Méndez and Christopher A. Neilson. School imagery and derived attributes prepared for the Manta, Ecuador school-choice study (“The Value of Choice in Centralized School Assignment”); imagery © respective sources as listed above.

This page documents the school imagery dataset assembled for our study of school choice in Manta, Ecuador. For each school we measure objective, parent-observable physical characteristics from satellite, street-level, and on-site photographs, and use them to give content to the otherwise unobserved component of school desirability in our demand model. The page describes what the imagery is, how it connects to the estimation, what it does and does not tell us, and the licensing under which each image source is used. The results are descriptive: the imagery names part of what makes schools attractive, and shows that most of it stays unobserved even with these richer measures—which is why the paper elicits preferences rather than proxying them.

1. The image types

Each school was photographed on-site (entrance, building, classrooms, courts, murals); the neighbourhood context is added from open Mapillary street imagery and Sentinel-2 satellite chips. Click any type to open a larger gallery and read how we interpret that view:

2. Embedding map

A vision model (CLIP) turns each image into a vector; we project to 2-D (PCA→t-SNE), so visually similar schools land near each other. Recolor by image type, or by a derived attribute (greenery / built-up density). Hover a point for its photo; click a point for its visual nearest neighbours.

3. How this connects to the demand estimation

Our demand model estimates how families trade off distance against school desirability. Administrative records contain very few school attributes, so most non-distance desirability is absorbed into a school-specific term, ξj, that the model treats as unobserved. That thinness raises an identification worry—separating a taste for proximity from a taste for quality needs some independent measure of what makes a school attractive—and a substantive question: how much of what families value could a planner observe from the outside?

From satellite imagery we measure building footprint, building count, built-up density and greenery; from ground and street-level photographs we code open recreation space, building condition, sidewalk quality, road quality, street-safety cues and commercial activity. These ten standardized attributes enter through a hierarchical prior on the school term, ξj ~ N(Xjβ, σξ2), so each coefficient is a willingness to travel in kilometres for a one-standard-deviation increase in the attribute, read against distance, the model's numeraire. Going beyond hand-coded attributes, we also embed each school's facade and interior photographs with a pre-trained vision model, following Compiani, Morozov and Seiler (2025), and enter the leading image dimensions directly as an additional desirability proxy.

What the imagery finds. The scale of the school plant carries a robust signal: a larger building footprint is worth about 0.4 km of extra travel, and a more fragmented campus (a higher building count) about 0.3 km less, both significant in all three grades; the other eight attributes are individually imprecise. The leading learned image dimension, which captures an open, low-density campus, is worth roughly 0.2–0.3 km per standard deviation and is significant in every grade. Allowing per-family random coefficients on two imagery indices—an urban built-up-scale index and a street-quality index—recovers economically meaningful taste heterogeneity in every grade (a standard deviation of 0.2–0.3 km on each index), so families do not treat schools as interchangeable conditional on distance. We do not over-read this as substitution: in a held-out exercise, image similarity to a family's first choice does not improve prediction of its second choice once distance is controlled.

What it does not find is the larger point. With ten imagery attributes and the learned image dimensions in the prior, most of the dispersion in ξj remains unexplained. Observable amenities do not substitute for elicited preferences: school desirability is real, large and largely idiosyncratic, so no parsimonious set of observable amenities can stand in for asking families directly. This is the measurement counterpart of the paper's central claim—a system that cannot see what families value has no proxy to fall back on. The same pipeline yields a second measurement result. Straight-line distance correlates 0.95 with Google-calibrated drive time on average, yet 28% of home–school pairs take more than 1.5 times, and 7% more than twice, the time their straight-line distance implies; re-estimating on the drive-time scale leaves the other parameters essentially unchanged but cuts the distance-taste heterogeneity σγ by 30–44% in every grade, so dispersion estimated under crow-flies distance is better read as an upper bound on genuine taste dispersion.

The attributes are generated regressors entered into the hierarchical prior, and the reported intervals do not propagate the uncertainty in deriving them from images, so individual coefficients are indicative rather than definitive; they price correlated bundles of quality, neighbourhood and price rather than isolated traits. Full estimates are in Section 5 and Appendix Table 14 of the paper.

4. Methods

Learned image features use a pre-trained CLIP ViT-B/32 vision encoder to embed facade, interior, and overhead photos; two-dimensional maps are produced by PCA followed by t-SNE for visualization only. Hand-coded attributes are produced by LLM-assisted coding with human verification of each value. Both the embeddings and the coded attributes enter the demand model as attributes in the hierarchical prior on school desirability (and, for two summary indices, with random coefficients), never as causal structural parameters. Because they are machine-generated, they are subject to the usual generated-regressor caution: coding error and imputation attenuate coefficients and the reported standard errors understate true uncertainty. The measurement results are reported in Section 5 of the paper (Figure 3 and Appendix Table 14); the headline welfare comparisons in Section 6 do not use the imagery attributes.

5. Data sources, licensing & privacy

Data sources and licensing

Imagery and derived attributes come from several sources, each used under its own terms:

  • On-site school photos (ConsiliumBots, Manta survey, December 2020): project-owned, restricted-use survey imagery, all rights reserved. Faces blurred before any public display. Photographs (c) ConsiliumBots; the face-blurred photos and all derived attributes (e.g. building condition) are publishable.
  • Mapillary street-level imagery: (c) Mapillary contributors, licensed under CC-BY-SA-4.0. Displayed tiles require attribution and share-alike; any public derivative imagery incorporating them is released under CC-BY-SA-4.0. This is our designated public street-level source.
  • Sentinel-2 satellite chips: contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (Sentinel-2); true-color chips and NDVI processed by the authors. Open data, displayed with Copernicus/ESA attribution. This is our designated public overhead source.
  • Derived geoscape attributes: school attributes derived by the authors from Overture Maps building footprints (CDLA-Permissive-2.0), Copernicus Sentinel-2 NDVI, and on-site/Mapillary imagery. These derived values are the shareable, publishable products.

Google imagery: derived attributes only, no tiles shown

Some attributes were coded internally with the help of Google Street View and Google satellite imagery, used for research only under the Google Maps/Street View Terms of Service. Per those terms, raw Google tiles are not stored publicly, redistributed, or shown on this page; no index is derived directly from the raw tiles. The public build displays only Mapillary street-level tiles, Sentinel-2 satellite tiles, and hand-verified derived attribute values. Where Google imagery informed a coded attribute, only the human/LLM-coded, hand-verified attribute value is reported, never the underlying tile. No published or derived result rests on Google tiles.

How to read these results

Coefficients are descriptive, not causal. Image attributes co-vary with unobserved school quality, neighbourhood composition and price, so they price correlated bundles rather than isolated traits. Two attributes—building footprint and building count—are significant in every grade; the finer ground-quality attributes are individually imprecise and are not interpreted as tastes. The willingness-to-travel figures come from the random-coefficient specification with a hierarchical prior on the school term, as in the paper's Table 14. The imagery does not drive the paper's welfare results: the headline comparison of the distance rule with deferred acceptance is estimated without it, and what the imagery adds is measurement—naming part of school appeal, showing that most of it remains unobserved, and revealing that a better travel-cost proxy absorbs a third to a half of the apparent dispersion in distance tastes. Attributes are coded from imagery with measurement error, span a 2016-earthquake vintage break, and enter as generated regressors whose derivation uncertainty is not propagated, so reported uncertainty is understated and individual coefficients should be read as indicative. The proximity benchmark also assumes the closest school is feasible, which it may not be if it is oversubscribed, sibling-linked or priority-ineligible.

Privacy.

All photographs shown are of public school buildings and grounds. Any incidental faces are automatically blurred before display. No personal, student, household, or other identifying data appears anywhere on this page; the imagery is used solely to characterize school facilities and their immediate surroundings.

(This build blurred 109 detected face regions; automated blurring is best-effort.)
